chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Hinton's St. Albans neighborhood and Fats Waller
summary: Hinton explains that the Queens neighborhood where they record was white and Fats Waller, Basie and others later lived nearby.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well, just while we're on this kind of thing, Butter, we might say that here we're in this basement here in St. Albans, Queens, --
And this community 40 years ago was a white community --
-- and Fats Waller lived right down the street, one block down the street.
From history, from what my white neighbors told me, he was the first black man to ever move in this neighborhood. And ironically later Basie bought a nice big house right across the street from him.

And then in later years Lena Horne moved out here and Jackie Robinson and Campanella and Ella Fitzgerald and Earl Bostick. So this community moved -- Babe Ruth was in this neighborhood in the early days when it was a white community. Babe -- It was a sportsmen's community where Babe Ruth lived, the great baseball player, Earl Sande, the great jockey.

And there was a white gentleman that lived around here. He was a dear friend of mine until he died. He was the last white person in this community. His name was Mr. Ellison. He lived right across the street from me and he would sit on my lawn. We'd sit out there and talk and he told me about the great times and the great poker games that they had with Babe Ruth and Earl Sande, --

-- and Fats Waller was welcomed in there and was accepted; being a great drinker and a great sportsman, he was in the midst of these poker games. I'd just like to interject that into your -- since we're talking about -- where we're doing this taping now right in this same community in 1976.
Uh-huh, uh-huh. Well, I'm glad to know that.
